rewrite.description: A four-part instrumental suite that moves from Garcia-like lead lines into denser, noisier electric passages, Solar Motel is Forsyth's move from solo-guitar Primitivism toward full-band, jam-length rock. It's less a set of songs than a single continuous guitar exploration, for listeners who like patient, building instrumental rock.

The Solar Motel Band's breakthrough tightens Forsyth's guitar suites into denser, riff-driven pieces, still stretching well past the length of a normal rock song. Interlocking electric leads and a steady rhythm section make it the most direct entry point into his band work.
rewrite.lineage: The full-band follow-up to Solar Motel, carrying Forsyth's Television- and Dead-indebted guitar vocabulary into tighter, riff-driven pieces.

rewrite.description: The former Beachwood Sparks multi-instrumentalist's solo debut is loose, sun-baked country-psych, heavy on steel guitar and warm analog fuzz. It sounds like an extension of the same Laurel Canyon-revival scene he helped build in his band work.
rewrite.lineage: A solo outlet for a Beachwood Sparks member, carrying that band's 2000s LA cosmic-country revival sound into looser, more psychedelic territory.

problems: contemporaneous-scene link is resemblance, not documented

rewrite.lineage: Beachwood Sparks returning to their Gram Parsons-descended sound at a moment when bands like Woods were working a similar Parsons/Dead vein, a parallel rather than a direct link.

problems: Terry cited as authority in lineage

rewrite.description: Georgia punks turned Dead-worshipping jammers, Arbor Labor Union's Sub Pop debut is fuzzed-out, repetitive guitar rock that treats a single riff as a launchpad for extended noise. It's the loudest, most distortion-caked branch of the cosmic-country revival covered here.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to Meat Puppets' punk-bred psychedelia and the Dead's long-form jamming, pushed toward drone and distortion.
Shows Arbor Labor Union moving from distortion-first jamming toward more structured songs that sound indebted to Dead- and Wilburys-style country rock.

rewrite.description: Yonder is Arbor Labor Union's most introspective, nocturnal record, cleaner and more inward than the kaleidoscopic New Petal Instants but no less indebted to the Allmans and Neil Young. Unhurried guitar lines wind around each other at walking tempos, suited to late-night listening.
rewrite.lineage: A quieter turn within Arbor Labor Union's catalog that still sounds drawn from the same Dead/Allman Brothers well as their earlier fuzzed-out records.

rewrite.description: A short follow-up EP to Yonder that keeps the same winding, left-field guitar grooves and Dead-indebted chord changes in a tighter package. The playing is crunchy and unpredictable, a quick fix for fans of the band's longer records.
rewrite.lineage: A compact continuation of Arbor Labor Union's post-Yonder sound, still sounding indebted to the Dead/Allman Brothers vein.

rewrite.description: Color Green's second album is a meditation on grief and clarity delivered through loose, live-feeling jams, from the hush of '5:08' to the sprawling 'Kick the Bucket.' Guitars trade lines and voices stack into harmonies the way a band that treats every gig as improvisation would.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to '60s SoCal folk-rock and the Dead/Allmans jam vocabulary, delivered with a live-band looseness.

rewrite.description: Cohen's fourth album, made with partner and producer Sam Evian at their Catskills studio Flying Cloud, is a hazy collage of memory built from years of home recording. Its soft-focus folk-pop favors atmosphere over hooks, with hushed vocals floating over gentle acoustic and keyboard textures.
rewrite.lineage: Grows out of the Flying Cloud/Sam Evian Catskills recording circle, the upstate-New York studio and label run by her partner.

rewrite.description: A gentle, warmly produced set of songs about distance and homecoming, Year Away favors soft-focus folk-pop arrangements over the twangier end of the C6 sound. It's closer to a hushed Laurel Canyon lullaby than a jam band, for listeners who want close harmonies and patient tempos.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds of a piece with the West Coast singer-songwriter circle around Anna St. Louis and Jess Williamson, sharing their soft-focus Laurel Canyon warmth.

problems: unverified member ties and track/runtime counts

rewrite.description: A debut LP from a loose LA collective, Aventurine spreads out into sprawling, heady grooves that recall electric-era Miles Davis and Can as much as the Dead. Its jam-length instrumental patience and synth textures put it at the far cosmic edge of this lane.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds like the cosmic-jam end of the scene stretched into krautrock and fusion territory, indebted to Can and electric Miles as much as the Dead.

problems: unverified album count, writing location and guest credit

rewrite.description: Streetsweeper is a tranquil, piano-and-guitar record from Andrews' long-running Yawns project. It's quieter and more contemplative than his fuller band records, closer to Little Wings' loose, handmade songwriting, for listeners who like soft-spoken, homespun songs.
rewrite.lineage: The latest entry in Andrews' long-running solo project, which sounds close to Little Wings' loose DIY songwriting.

problems: formation story wrong: made for Fare Thee Well set-break music, not a box set

rewrite.description: Formed by the late Neal Casal to play set-break music for the Grateful Dead's 2015 Fare Thee Well concerts before becoming its own band, this self-titled third LP pushes the instrumental jam group toward a groovier, cosmic-disco direction. It's an all-instrumental record that wears its Dead pedigree (bassist Dan Horne also plays in Beachwood Sparks) openly.

St. Louis's second album opens up her stark debut into brighter, more orchestral arrangements of strings, piano and fingerpicked guitar. It trades the gritty apparitions of her first record for patient, present-tense contentment, sung in her low, unhurried voice.
rewrite.lineage: Connects directly to the Woodsist label that released her debut, and sounds of a piece with the West Coast singer-songwriter circle of Jess Williamson and Kacey Johansing.

rewrite.description: A deliberately harder-to-parse record than Walker's earlier Fahey-descended guitar albums, Deafman Glance buries his songwriting under synths, warped studio effects and loose improvisational playing from Chicago's experimental scene. Songs like 'In Castle Dome' drift and fracture rather than resolve, for listeners who like folk-rock with a free-jazz streak.

New Jersey's Garcia Peoples keep working the dual-guitar-jam vein of their earlier records, all extended solos and interlocking leads in the spirit of the guitarist their name nods to. It's dense, riff-forward psych-jam rock built for headphones or a long drive.
rewrite.lineage: Takes its name from Jerry Garcia and sounds directly indebted to his lead style and the Dead's long-form jamming.
Ethan Miller's move from the noisier Comets on Fire into a more classic-rock sound that is indebted to Crazy Horse and the Allman Brothers, launching his long-running Howlin Rain project.

rewrite.description: Silverstein alternates expansive pedal-steel-laced instrumentals with songs sung in a delivery pitched between Bill Callahan's deadpan and Kurt Vile's drift. It's cosmic country in the vein of Beachwood Sparks and Silver Jews, slow and sunlit.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds of a piece with the Pacific Northwest cosmic-country instrumentalists around Rose City Band, sharing their pedal-steel drift.

rewrite.description: Baggett makes crunchy, warm Crazy Horse-style rock here, all snaking guitar solos and B3 organ. It sits comfortably alongside the mellower, jam-friendly end of this lane, for listeners who like their fuzz relaxed.
rewrite.lineage: Sounds indebted to Crazy Horse's loose guitar rock, filtered through the relaxed sensibility of West Coast lo-fi songwriters like Little Wings.
